body: I think this is fine. I suspect most areas won't have a visual difference anyway. But this needs to be tested before being merged

One thing to look out for when reviewing and testing this PR:

Calculating true luminance can accidentally cause clipping in higher value channels. This is specifically an issue in tonemapping, so calculating luminance as simply the max of the three colour channels (like Godot does before this PR) avoids this potential clipping issue.

I have not inspected the code of this PR, but a description of where the true luminance calculation can fail is described under the ["Luminance Only" heading of this page](http://filmicworlds.com/blog/filmic-tonemapping-with-piecewise-power-curves/).

**Edit:** After re-reading, I noticed the linked example doesn't exactly match this true luminance equation, so here's an example that fits this scenario better:

- `RGB(0.1, 0.1, 1.0) luminance = 0.16498`
- Apply an adjustment to luminance, such as one that scales this luminance up slightly to `0.2` while keeping it within the `[0, 1]` range, for example.
- Figure out the luminance ratio: `0.2 / 0.16498 = 1.2123`
- Apply the ratio to the original value: `= RGB(0.21, 0.21, 1.21)`.
- Now blue is clipping in SDR, even though you kept luminance nicely within the `[0, 1]` range.

This sort of thing can happen with a tonemapping curve for certain values if the tonemapping curve is calculated based on the true luminance. This can be avoided by using the max values, even though that is obviously not a correct luminance calculation.

It may be possible that some existing uses of the incorrect max-channel-"luminance" calculation have depended on the current behaviour to avoid sudden hard clipping of a channel. I can look into this a bit more sometime in the next while, but figured I'd highlight this point sooner rather than later.

(Obviously none of this applies to correcting the luminance calculations that were simply using the wrong coefficients: if they clip, they've always clipped, so it's not going to introduce a new issue.)

I took a more conservative approach to this PR and only replaced the clearly incorrect luminance weights with the correct ones:

[0001-Replace-NTSC-PAL-luminance-weights-0.299-0.587-0.114.patch](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/22622365/0001-Replace-NTSC-PAL-luminance-weights-0.299-0.587-0.114.patch)

This approach does not make any assumptions regarding the places where even weights or other approaches are being used; it only replaces the obviously incorrect NTSC/PAL luminance weights with Rec. 709 luminance weights. It also makes it clear in the code that these are Rec. 709 luminance weights to allow for easier [adapting to other weights in the future](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/12783).

But I hit a bit of a challenge when doing this: the hue rotation code used in particles has some more complex colour math that is based on NTSC/PAL luminance weights that needs to be updated. I don't know how to re-generate these rotations based on the correct luminance weights, but I did find a [source that describes the process that was used](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/direct2d/hue-rotate). If anyone is able to correctly regenerate the hue rotation code to use the correct Rec. 709 luminance weights, please also do the work to make the hue rotation code for other colours:

**Rec. 709:** `(0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722)` (rounded from: `(0.212639005871510, 0.715168678767756, 0.072192315360734)`)
**P3:** `(0.228974564069749, 0.691738521836506, 0.079286914093745)`
**Rec. 2020**: `(0.262700212011267, 0.677998071518871, 0.059301716469862)`

I'll eventually revisit this and this PR still likely serves a purpose of exploring some places where the codebase uses the term "luminance" to loosely describe something other than CIE relative luminance...
